summary: Single-author case study in which Claude Code (Opus 4.7, Lean 4) under the author's supervision implements three simple compiler optimizations (UCE, DAE, CP) twice in the author's own agent-built Axon compiler: once as credible compilation (unverified transform + verified certificate checker) and once fully verified. It reports effort (sessions, active time, tokens, LoC, prompts) and compile-time statistics, concluding verification costs about an order of magnitude more effort.

claims.claim: Verification requires roughly an order of magnitude more development effort than credible compilation.
claims.evidence: Table 1: UCE CC 1 session / 0:18 / 0.49M tokens vs UCE VF 8 sessions / 5:58 / 12.27M tokens; CP CC 1.75M tokens vs CP VF 17.86M tokens; UCE+DAE CC 1.86M vs VF 16.35M; proof LoC +4,348 to +8,158 for VF vs +0 for CC. Ratios hold, but each cell is a single supervised development run (n=1) with one supervisor and one model; checker-update (CU) rows partly offset the CC side.

claims.claim: To enhance provability the agent chose less efficient algorithms/data structures, making verified optimizations slower.
claims.evidence: Table 2 timings (20 runs, min/max dropped, mean of 18; SDs in Tables 3-4) show VF slower than CC opt; attribution to lists-vs-hash-maps and whole-program fixed-point iteration is qualitative (§5, §6).

claims.claim: The agent repeatedly reduced optimization scope to minimise proof effort.
claims.evidence: Narrative development histories in §5.1-5.3; no systematic count beyond anecdotes.

claims.claim: Certificate checking time dominates optimization and certificate generation time.
claims.evidence: Table 2 chk column vs opt/gen on Livermore kernels; consistent with prior Axon report (ref 23, same author).

claims.claim: Formal specs + verified checker eliminate the need for human code audits and enable immediately deployable agent code.
claims.evidence: Asserted in §1 and §6; no audit-vs-no-audit comparison, no defect study. The corpus paper 2607.28928 runs automated testing/repair on the same Axon compiler, implying defects outside verified code.

patterns.note: Agent produced full Lean proofs and verified checkers for three optimizations; feasibility demonstrated, but at ~10x effort for full verification.
Credible compilation is an execution-time checker gate: unverified agent output accepted only if verified certificate check passes; this was the cheap path.
All work done under human supervision with prompt counts reported (1-59 per optimization); supervision cost grows sharply for verification.
Reports tokens and cache reads per task (Table 1) but no budget/cap mechanism.

methodology.sample: 3 optimizations x 2 approaches, each developed once (n=1 per cell), plus checker-update rows; compile timing on Livermore kernels (20 runs each).
methodology.baselines: Credible compilation vs full verification compared against each other; no human-developer baseline or other agent/model.
methodology.models: Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context), single model.
methodology.variance: Timing: SDs reported (Tables 3-4). Effort metrics: none (single run, single supervisor).
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a (new Lean code); data collection scripts were themselves agent-generated (§4).
methodology.languages: Lean 4; Axon TAC IR; Livermore kernels auto-translated from Fortran.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint, no venue listed in comment or journal_ref.
standards.artifacts: No code/data link in text or metadata; initial prompts given in §11.

biases.detail: Author evaluates development on his own Axon compiler (ref 23, Rinard 2026) and his own supervision; all measurement scripts were agent-generated.
Three simple optimizations, each implemented once per approach; effort numbers are single trajectories.
Only Claude Opus 4.7 via Claude Code; limitations admit another supervisor/agent could change results.
No repeated development runs; effort ratios have no uncertainty.
Claims of eliminating human code audits and 'immediately deployable components with no required human validation' go beyond evidence.
No repository link for Axon or the optimization code in this paper.

coi.affiliations: Martin Rinard, National University of Singapore and MIT (single author).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code / Claude Opus 4.7 used as tool, not the object of comparison; Axon compiler is the author's own system.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding statement found.
coi.detail: Academic author; no vendor affiliation. Self-evaluation of own system and approach preference (credible compilation) is an intellectual, not commercial, conflict.

verdict_reason: Effort ratios in Table 1 do back the order-of-magnitude claim, but it is n=1 per cell, single model, single supervisor, on the author's own toy-language compiler; the 'no audits needed' conclusion is unsupported.
applicability: Indirect. The transferable lesson for a Java backend team is architectural: let agents write unverified transforms but gate them with a cheap, trusted checker (schema/contract validators for incoming text, golden-file diff checks) rather than demanding proofs of the transform itself. That pairs well with spec-driven development if specs are machine-checkable (JSON Schema/OpenAPI contracts shared across the several repositories). Lean proofs and compiler IR do not transfer to Spring/Java services, and effort numbers are tied to one Claude host, so they say nothing about mixed agent hosts.

conflicts_with.detail: Applies automated defect detection and agent repair to the same Axon compiler (noting possible reward hacking risk from validation on a small benchmark set), which tempers this paper's claim that the formal architecture removes the need for code audits.
